To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the failure of colostral transfer of immunoglobulins is a major cause of neonatal calf mortality.
failure in passive immunoglobulin transfer, as reflected in low serum IgG1, is a significant risk factor in the death of neonatal calves from infectious disease.
failure of colostral IgG transfer in calves less than three weeks old dying from infectious disease was associated with significantly lower (P<0.01) serum IgG1 than in clinically normal calves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the immune system in the pathogenesis of disease.
the effects of colostral transfer on the immune system of the neonatal calf and the relationship between failure of passive transfer and neonatal calf disease.
the development of an effective vaccine to prevent neonatal calf diarrhea (NCD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most important factor in neonatal calf mortality is failure of the calf to receive adequate colostral immunoglobin.
failure of colostral Ig transfer is a major cause of death in neonatal calves.
failure in passive immunoglobulin transfer is an important contributing factor in the pathogenesis of disease in calves dying from infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the failure of colostral Ig transfer was a significant cause of neonatal calf mortality in the United States.
calves dying of infectious disease have low IgG1 concentrations and that this low IgG1 is due to failure in colostral transfer.
failure of passive transfer is the most important cause of neonatal calf mortality and morbidity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
failure in passive immunity in calves is a major factor contributing to mortality.
failure of passive transfer is a major factor in neonatal mortality.
we should be doing a better job of ensuring that calves get adequate colostrum.
